passage: Every Diwali, when the lamps were lit and the sweets came out, Dada Varun told the story again. "The night Harsha was born, the lane was flooded up to the knees. Your father couldn't find an auto, so I walked ahead with the torch, and he carried the bag, and we waded through all the way to the hospital." Harsha mouthed the words along with him, knowing every pause. Cousins rolled their eyes, but Harsha never did. It felt like a rope tied to something solid. "And then you arrived, right on time, hungry and loud," finished Dada. Harsha sat a little straighter every time.

qa.q: What was the lane like the night Harsha was born?
How does Harsha feel each time Dada Varun tells the story?
qa.a: Proud and a sense of belonging. Harsha knows every pause, mouths the words and sits straighter, as if tied to something solid.

qa.q: How could the family keep the story helpful for Harsha as time goes by?
qa.a: By letting Harsha add a part to the telling or ask questions about it, so the story stays about a family that pulls together, not only about the past.

qa.q: How might the cousins see the story differently from Harsha?
qa.a: They may hear it as an old story they have heard many times, while for Harsha it carries a place in the family, as shown by their eye-rolling.

grounding: A child hears the family story of their birth repeatedly and feels a place and sense of belonging.

passage:
"Dada, tell me the shop story," said Divyansh.
"You have heard it a hundred times," said Chinmay.
"Tell it again. Please?"
"Fine. When I was your age, I walked six kilometres each day to school. Then I saved my first coins and opened a little shop, with one shelf and a scale."
"And the sign?"
"I painted it myself, crooked." Dada laughed.
"Today in class," said Divyansh, "the teacher asked what our family does. I said we open the shop before sunrise, and we fix the crooked sign every year."
Chinmay looked at Divyansh for a long moment. "Yes. That's us."

qa.q: How far did Chinmay walk to school each day?
What was Divyansh feeling when telling the class about the family shop?
qa.a: Pride and belonging. Divyansh spoke of the shop and the crooked sign as "we," as if part of the story.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make at the start of the conversation?
qa.a: Chinmay agreed to tell the shop story again, even after a hundred tellings, and shared the details of the shelf, the scale and the crooked sign.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have felt when Divyansh said "we open the shop before sunrise"?
qa.a: Moved and proud, because Divyansh had taken the story on as part of who the family is; Chinmay looked for a long moment and said "That's us."

grounding: A child repeatedly hears what Dada did and feels part of the family through it.
